python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path('docs/ai-dev.md')
s = p.read_text()

section = '''## Hermes infrastructure agent

Hermes manages infrastructure, and it reads input nobody controls: web pages
through its bundled browser, and container logs, which are strings written by
whatever produced them. It therefore runs as its own `hermes` account, not as
the management user. `/home/michael` is mode `0750`, so the agent cannot read
the management user's GitHub tokens, SSH keys, or Claude and Codex sessions.
That separation is the point: scoping the agent's own credentials achieves
nothing while broader credentials sit beside it in the same home directory.

Ansible owns the account, installs the agent with `--skip-setup`, and deploys
its credentials. The installer clones `NousResearch/hermes-agent` into
`~/.hermes/hermes-agent`, builds a uv virtualenv, links `~/.local/bin/hermes`,
and pulls a Hermes-managed Node and a Playwright browser, so the first run is
long and the install is the largest on the VM. ai-dev installs the Docker
client for `DOCKER_HOST` queries but masks `docker.service` and
`docker.socket`; it must never run a daemon of its own.

### Access tiers

The agent observes broadly, acts narrowly, and proposes everything else.

| Tier | Reach | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Observe | Proxmox cluster and guest state; Docker containers, logs, stats, events | `PVEAuditor` API token; read-only socket proxy |
| Propose | Any change to this repository | Fine-grained GitHub token, pull request only |
| Act | Nothing on a running host | Deliberately absent |

No credential the agent holds can change a running host. Remediation happens
by pull request, which `main`'s branch protection forces through review, and
which Portainer then deploys. A merge is the supervision that a watched SSH
session used to provide.

### Provisioning the credentials

Mint the Proxmox audit identity on the hypervisor. `PVEAuditor` is read-only by
construction, and privilege separation keeps the token's grant explicit:

```sh
ssh root@proxmox
pveum user add hermes-audit@pve --comment 'Read-only audit for ai-dev Hermes'
pveum acl modify / --users hermes-audit@pve --roles PVEAuditor
pveum user token add hermes-audit@pve ai-dev --privsep 1
pveum acl modify / --tokens 'hermes-audit@pve!ai-dev' --roles PVEAuditor
```

The token value prints once. Create the GitHub token in the GitHub UI, because
fine-grained tokens cannot be minted through the API: scope it to
`mich-murphy/home-infra` alone, grant Contents and Pull requests read/write,
and grant nothing else. Then store both in the vault:

```sh
cd ansible
ansible-vault edit group_vars/secrets.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass
```

```yaml
hermes_proxmox_token_id: "hermes-audit@pve!ai-dev"
hermes_proxmox_token_secret: "<token value>"
hermes_github_token: "<fine-grained token>"
```

The play installs the agent without these and reports their absence, so the
host can be provisioned before the tokens exist. With them present it writes
`~hermes/.config/hermes/env` at mode `0600`, sourced from the account's
`.profile`.

### Operating it

```sh
sudo -u hermes -i
hermes setup
hermes --version
hermes update
```

Ansible installs the agent but does not update it; `hermes update` follows
`origin/main` of the upstream repository. That is an unpinned, self-updating
code path, which is acceptable on a disposable DMZ guest and is a reason the
agent lives here rather than on docker-host.

### Known exposure

The Docker socket proxy filters which requests are allowed, not what the
answers contain. `GET /containers/{id}/json` returns a container's environment
block, so the agent can read the Cloudflare DNS token, the Pocket ID
encryption key, and application API keys on docker-host. Removing that
exposure means moving those values out of Compose `environment:` entries, not
tightening the proxy. Treat the agent's credentials as revocable and rotate
them if ai-dev is ever suspect: delete the Proxmox token with
`pveum user token remove hermes-audit@pve ai-dev`, and revoke the GitHub token
in the GitHub UI.

'''

anchor = "## Plannotator remote reviews"
assert s.count(anchor) == 1
s = s.replace(anchor, section + anchor)

old_policy = """Replace `group:ai-dev-users` with the tailnet's approved selectors. Do not add a
grant with `tag:ai-dev` as a source; grants are additive, so a broader existing
grant can defeat this containment."""
new_policy = """Replace `group:ai-dev-users` with the tailnet's approved selectors. Grants are
additive, so a broader existing grant can defeat this containment.

The Hermes agent requires the single exception below: ai-dev as a source,
reaching one read-only port on docker-host and the Proxmox API. Keep it this
narrow. Any wider grant with `tag:ai-dev` as a source erases the separation the
guest exists to provide.

```json
{
  "grants": [
    {
      "src": ["tag:ai-dev"],
      "dst": ["docker-host"],
      "ip": ["tcp:2375"]
    },
    {
      "src": ["tag:ai-dev"],
      "dst": ["proxmox"],
      "ip": ["tcp:8006"]
    }
  ]
}
```

The Docker port is pinned a second time in docker-host's `DOCKER-USER` chain,
so a mistake in this policy alone does not expose the Docker API."""
assert s.count(old_policy) == 1
s = s.replace(old_policy, new_policy)
p.write_text(s)
print("ok")

interfaces. An empty `AGENT_PROXY_BIND` would make Compose bind everywhere,
so the bind address is verified rather than assumed.

a container's environment block, so the agent can read secrets passed through

the only fix; no proxy setting achieves it.

Everything's built and passing. Here's where it stands.

**Done and verified**

`main` is protected — PR required with one approval, force pushes and deletions blocked, linear history. That closed the live path where anything on ai-dev could push a compose file and have Portainer deploy it.

On ai-dev, Hermes moved out of `michael`'s toolchain into its own `hermes` account (`ansible/roles/ai-dev/tasks/hermes.yaml`). It gets its own home at mode `0750`, a locked password, and its credentials in `~/.config/hermes/env` at `0600`. The role asserts `/home/michael` stays `0750` rather than trusting it, since that one permission bit is what keeps the agent away from your GitHub tokens, SSH keys, and Claude/Codex sessions. It installs the Docker client for `DOCKER_HOST` queries and masks `docker.service` and `docker.socket`, with an assertion that the mask holds — ai-dev must not run a daemon. Credentials are optional: the play installs and reports what's missing, so it runs cleanly before the tokens exist.

On docker-host, `docker/init/compose.yml` gains a second instance of the same pinned proxy image with `POST=0` and only the read routes needed to diagnose. Ansible reads the host's Tailscale address at deploy time into `AGENT_PROXY_BIND`, and `DOCKER-USER` now admits one source address on 2375 and drops everyone else. I found a sharp edge worth knowing: if `AGENT_PROXY_BIND` is ever empty, Compose binds *every* interface silently, so `verify.yaml` asserts the container never binds `0.0.0.0` and both roles assert their tailnet addresses resolved.

All checks pass: `ansible-lint` at production profile, playbook syntax, shellcheck, the maintenance test, every compose file rendering, and the Portainer drift check. I added `AGENT_PROXY_BIND` to the CI env block so the docker gate renders a realistic bind.

**Two things I changed that you should look at**

`docs/ai-dev.md` said never to add a tailnet grant with `tag:ai-dev` as a source. This design needs exactly that, so I documented it as a narrow, explicit exception — ai-dev to docker-host `tcp:2375` and Proxmox `tcp:8006`, nothing else — rather than quietly contradicting the rule. That's a real loosening of a policy you wrote deliberately, and it deserves your eye.

I also documented the env-var exposure in both docs as a known, accepted limitation, since you said "ideally not" and the proxy can't deliver that ideal.

**What's left for you**

The Proxmox commands are still blocked — auto mode refused state-changing SSH to `root@proxmox` twice, so the audit user doesn't exist yet. The exact commands are in `docs/ai-dev.md` under "Provisioning the credentials". Then create the fine-grained PAT in the GitHub UI scoped to `home-infra` with Contents and Pull requests only, add both to the vault, and add the tailnet grants. Nothing is deployed yet — this is all working-tree changes, nothing has run against a host.

Want me to open this as a PR? That would be the first real exercise of the branch protection, which is worth proving works before you rely on it.

### Reaching the agent

The account is a normal login. Ansible authorizes the same operator key that
reaches the management user and enables linger, so the account can hold its
own persistent Herdr and Moshi services. Either path works:

```sh
ssh hermes@ai-dev          # dedicated session, own Herdr and Moshi
sudo -u hermes -i          # from an existing management-user pane
```

Prefer the dedicated SSH session when the agent should keep long-running work
alive independently of the management user's Herdr, which is the usual case
for infrastructure monitoring. Use `sudo -u hermes -i` for a quick look from a
pane that is already open.

Each account runs its own Herdr and Moshi. Pair Moshi separately for `hermes`
if the agent should reach the phone; the management user's pairing does not
carry across, and that separation is intentional.

Authorizing the operator key grants a human entry into the agent account. It
grants the agent nothing: no key on the agent's side reaches the management
user, whose home stays mode `0750`.

hermes setup
hermes --version
hermes update
```

Yes — `ssh hermes@ai-dev`, and I've made that work properly rather than leaving you to `sudo` your way in.

**Answering the question directly:** you have two paths now.

`ssh hermes@ai-dev` gives the agent account a dedicated session with its own Herdr and Moshi. I added your operator key to `~hermes/.ssh/authorized_keys` and enabled linger, so that account can hold persistent user services the way `michael` does. This is the one you want for infrastructure monitoring, where the agent's work should survive independently of your coding sessions.

`sudo -u hermes -i` still works for a quick look from a pane you already have open, and needs nothing extra since `michael` is in `wheel`.

Three things worth knowing about the shape of this. The two accounts run *separate* Herdr and Moshi instances — your existing Moshi pairing doesn't carry across, so if you want Hermes reaching your phone you pair Moshi again as `hermes`. That's the separation working as intended, not an oversight. The direction of trust also stays one-way: authorizing your key lets *you* into the agent account, but gives the agent nothing back — `/home/michael` remains `0750` and no key on the agent's side points at you. And no firewall change was needed, since this is the same port 22 you already reach over Tailscale.

I also changed the credential logic while I was there: it originally deployed all three secrets or none, which would have left your working Proxmox token idle until the GitHub PAT existed. content.text:
Confirmed on the live host, and the premise needs correcting: you aren't using Tailscale SSH.

ai-dev reports `"RunSSH": false`. Tailscale SSH is deliberately off — `identity.yaml` runs `tailscale set --ssh=false` and asserts it stays off, and `docs/ai-dev.md` states it as policy. What you're actually doing with `ssh michael@ai-dev` is ordinary OpenSSH: MagicDNS resolves `ai-dev` to its tailnet address, and normal `sshd` on port 22 authenticates your key. Tailscale is carrying the packets, not handling the auth.

Which is good news for your question. Because auth is `authorized_keys`, `ssh hermes@ai-dev` works exactly like `ssh michael@ai-dev`, with no extra setup beyond what I already added. I checked the specifics:

- `sshd` has no `AllowUsers`, `AllowGroups`, or `DenyUsers` restriction, so it isn't scoped to `michael` — any account with an authorized key can log in.
- Effective config is `PubkeyAuthentication yes`, `PasswordAuthentication no`, `AuthenticationMethods publickey`. The `hermes` account has `password_lock: true`, which is fine: key auth is the only path anyway.
- The role writes the same `ssh_public_key` variable into `~hermes/.ssh/authorized_keys` that `common/users.yaml` writes into `michael`'s. Same key, same client, no new tailnet grant — `tcp:22` already covers it.

Worth noting the distinction matters if you ever reconsider: had you been on Tailscale SSH, access would be governed by tailnet ACL `ssh` rules and `authorized_keys` would be bypassed entirely, so the agent account's reachability would live in the tailnet policy instead of on the host. Turning it on would also fail the play, since `identity.yaml` asserts `RunSSH` is false.

So: nothing more to do for access. It'll work after the next deploy, once the account exists.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Tailscale SSH, Mosh support, port forwarding, and limitations:

## Port Forwarding Limitations

Tailscale SSH doesn't support the "-L" or "-R" flags commonly used for port forwarding. This is a significant limitation, as no documentation exists on the state of port forwarding using tailscale ssh, although empirically, it doesn't work.

## Mosh Support with Tailscale

There is a known compatibility issue between Mosh and Tailscale SSH. Tailscale SSH isn't real OpenSSH, so Mosh can't bootstrap through it, but installing OpenSSH alongside Tailscale makes everything work. Specifically, Tailscale SSH has hijacked port 22, which interferes with Mosh's connection handshake.

The recommended approach is handing port 22 back to the OS sshd so key auth works for Moshi and every other SSH client, and mosh can bootstrap.

## Port Forwarding for Port Forwarding

If you need port forwarding capabilities, use SSH for scripts, file transfer, and port forwarding, and keep it separate from your Mosh session.

---
# Hermes manages infrastructure and reads untrusted input (web pages via its
# bundled browser, and container logs). It therefore runs as its own account so
# that a compromised agent cannot reach the management user's GitHub
# credentials, SSH keys, or coding-agent sessions.
- name: Create the Hermes agent group
  ansible.builtin.group:
    name: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    state: present

- name: Create the Hermes agent user
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    group: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    home: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}"
    shell: /bin/bash
    create_home: true
    password_lock: true

# The management user's home is mode 0750 (common role). Hermes is outside that
# group, so this is the control that keeps the agent away from the human's
# credentials. Assert it rather than assume it.
- name: Read the management user home directory state
  ansible.builtin.stat:
    path: "/home/{{ username }}"
  register: ai_dev_management_home

- name: Verify the Hermes user cannot read the management user's home
  ansible.builtin.assert:
    that:
      - ai_dev_management_home.stat.mode is version('0750', '<=')
      - ai_dev_management_home.stat.pw_name == username
    fail_msg: >-
      /home/{{ username }} must stay owner-private so the Hermes account cannot
      read the management user's GitHub tokens, SSH keys, or agent sessions.

- name: Keep the Hermes home directory owner-private
  ansible.builtin.file:
    path: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}"
    state: directory
    owner: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    group: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    mode: "0750"

- name: Ensure the Hermes SSH directory exists
  ansible.builtin.file:
    path: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}/.ssh"
    state: directory
    owner: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    group: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    mode: "0700"

# The human authenticates into the agent account; the agent holds no key that
# reaches back the other way.
- name: Authorize the operator key for the Hermes account
  ansible.builtin.copy:
    content: "{{ ssh_public_key }}\n"
    dest: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}/.ssh/authorized_keys"
    owner: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    group: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    mode: "0600"

- name: Enable linger for persistent Hermes user services
  ansible.builtin.command:
    cmd: "loginctl enable-linger {{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
  args:
    creates: "/var/lib/systemd/linger/{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"

- name: Ensure the Hermes user-local executable directory exists
  ansible.builtin.file:
    path: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}/.local/bin"
    state: directory
    owner: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    group: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    mode: "0755"

# Provides the docker client for DOCKER_HOST queries against the docker-host
# socket proxy. ai-dev must never run its own daemon, so it stays masked.
- name: Install the Docker client
  community.general.pacman:
    name: docker
    state: present

- name: Mask the local Docker daemon and socket
  ansible.builtin.systemd_service:
    name: "{{ item }}"
    enabled: false
    masked: true
    state: stopped
  loop:
    - docker.service
    - docker.socket

- name: Install the Hermes agent
  ansible.builtin.shell:
    cmd: >-
      curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh
      | bash -s -- --skip-setup
  args:
    creates: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}/.local/bin/hermes"
  become: true
  become_user: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
  environment:
    HOME: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}"
    USER: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    PATH: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}/.local/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin"

- name: Ensure the Hermes configuration directory exists
  ansible.builtin.file:
    path: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}/.config/hermes"
    state: directory
    owner: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    group: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    mode: "0700"

# Scoped credentials only. The Proxmox token carries PVEAuditor, the GitHub
# token is resource-scoped to this repository with contents and pull-request
# write, and the Docker endpoint is a read-only socket proxy. None of them
# grant write access to a running host.
- name: Deploy the Hermes scoped credential environment
  ansible.builtin.copy:
    content: |
      DOCKER_HOST={{ ai_dev_hermes_docker_host }}
      PROXMOX_ENDPOINT={{ ai_dev_hermes_proxmox_endpoint }}
      {% if ai_dev_hermes_proxmox_credentials_present %}
      PROXMOX_TOKEN_ID={{ hermes_proxmox_token_id }}
      PROXMOX_TOKEN_SECRET={{ hermes_proxmox_token_secret }}
      {% endif %}
      {% if ai_dev_hermes_github_credentials_present %}
      GH_TOKEN={{ hermes_github_token }}
      GITHUB_TOKEN={{ hermes_github_token }}
      {% endif %}
    dest: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}/.config/hermes/env"
    owner: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    group: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    mode: "0600"
  no_log: true

- name: Report Hermes credentials still missing from the vault
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: >-
      Hermes is installed without
      {{ _ai_dev_hermes_missing | join(' and ') }} access. Add the matching
      variables to group_vars/secrets.yaml and re-run.
  vars:
    _ai_dev_hermes_missing: >-
      {{ (['Proxmox'] if not ai_dev_hermes_proxmox_credentials_present else [])
         + (['GitHub'] if not ai_dev_hermes_github_credentials_present else []) }}
  when: _ai_dev_hermes_missing | length > 0

- name: Load the scoped credentials into the Hermes login environment
  ansible.builtin.copy:
    content: |
      # Managed by Ansible (ai-dev role). Scoped agent credentials.
      if [ -r "$HOME/.config/hermes/env" ]; then
          set -a
          . "$HOME/.config/hermes/env"
          set +a
      fi
      PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
      export PATH
    dest: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}/.profile"
    owner: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    group: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    mode: "0644"

- name: Read the installed Hermes version
  ansible.builtin.command:
    argv:
      - "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}/.local/bin/hermes"
      - --version
  become: true
  become_user: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
  environment:
    HOME: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}"
    USER: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_user }}"
    PATH: "{{ ai_dev_hermes_home }}/.local/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin"
  register: ai_dev_hermes_version
  changed_when: false
  when: not ansible_check_mode

- name: Verify the Hermes agent responds
  ansible.builtin.assert:
    that:
      - ai_dev_hermes_version.stdout | length > 0
    fail_msg: The Hermes agent did not report a version.
  when: not ansible_check_mode

- name: Read the local Docker daemon state
  ansible.builtin.command:
    argv:
      - /usr/bin/systemctl
      - is-enabled
      - docker.service
  register: ai_dev_docker_daemon_state
  changed_when: false
  failed_when: false
  when: not ansible_check_mode

- name: Verify ai-dev runs no local Docker daemon
  ansible.builtin.assert:
    that:
      - "'masked' in ai_dev_docker_daemon_state.stdout"
    fail_msg: >-
      ai-dev must not run a local Docker daemon; docker.service must stay
      masked so the client only reaches the docker-host socket proxy.
  when: not ansible_check_mode

1	# AI development VM
2	
3	`ai-dev` is the single AI development VM. It retains Proxmox VMID 110 and its
4	150 GB disk, with 4 CPU cores, fixed 5 GiB RAM, and an 8 GiB disk-backed
5	swapfile with a bounded zswap cache. Its only NIC is on the physical `vmbr1`
6	DMZ.
7	
8	The supported remote path is:
9	
10	```text
11	Moshi -> Tailscale private network -> OpenSSH -> Mosh when available -> Herdr
12	```
13	
14	Tailscale SSH stays disabled, and this is load-bearing rather than incidental.
15	Tailscale SSH is not OpenSSH: it takes over port 22, so Mosh cannot bootstrap
16	through it, and it does not implement `-L`/`-R` port forwarding, which
17	Plannotator reviews and Moshi's Browser Preview both depend on. Moshi's own
18	documentation recommends leaving it off so port 22 returns to the OS `sshd`.
19	Enabling it would break the path above and fail the identity assertions in the
20	ai-dev role.
21	
22	Disabling it costs nothing in key handling. Moshi's Easy Pair appends its own
23	public key to the target account's `authorized_keys` during pairing, so no
24	private key is ever pasted into the phone. Ansible manages only its own
25	operator key line, leaving Moshi's entry intact.
26	
27	Moshi connects to the guest's normal OpenSSH server through Tailscale, then
28	uses Mosh's per-connection UDP server when the network permits it. Herdr is the only persistent multiplexer and retains its
29	shared `Ctrl-A` prefix. `Ctrl+Shift+L` is encoded as F12 by a supporting
30	terminal, forwarded by Herdr, and bound by Fish to clear the focused pane.
31	
32	## Deployment
33	
34	The existing guest initially advertises the old `ai-dev-bgd` MagicDNS name. For
35	the first Ansible run only, temporarily set the inventory line to:
36	
37	```ini
38	ai-dev ansible_host=ai-dev-bgd ansible_user=michael
39	```
40	
41	Run the AI host play, verify that Linux and Tailscale both advertise `ai-dev`,
42	then restore the committed inventory line without `ansible_host`. Do not leave
43	the migration alias in steady state.
44	
45	Before planning or applying Terraform, rotate any Tailscale authentication key
46	that was rendered into an old local cloud-init file. Remove the old
47	`terraform/files/ai-dev-bc.cfg` and `terraform/files/ai-dev-bgd.cfg` files after
48	rotation. They are ignored generated artifacts and must not be treated as a
49	credential store.
50	
51	Run:
52	
53	```sh
54	cd terraform
55	terraform fmt -check -recursive
56	terraform validate
57	terraform plan
58	```
59	
60	The plan must report the address move from
61	`module.ai_dev["ai-dev-bgd"]` to `module.ai_dev`, followed by an in-place rename
62	and CPU/memory update. Stop if VMID 110 or its disk would be destroyed or
63	replaced.
64	If the plan instead proposes creating all BPG-provider VMs or asks for the
65	legacy Telmate provider, stop: the local state predates the earlier provider
66	migration and must be reconciled/imported before this rename can be planned.
67	
68	Then stage the guest and router changes:
69	
70	```sh
71	cd ansible
72	ansible-playbook run.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass \
73	  --limit ai-dev --check --diff
74	ansible-playbook run.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass --limit ai-dev
75	ansible-playbook run.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass --limit ai-dev
76	cd ..
77	just routeros
78	```
79	
80	The ai-dev role clones the public `nix-config` repository to
81	`/home/michael/dev/nix-config`, fast-forwards it to `origin/main`, builds
82	`homeConfigurations."michael@ai-dev"`, and activates it as `michael`. A
83	non-fast-forward checkout or conflicting local change stops deployment.
84	Check mode builds the activation package but never activates it.
85	
86	Home Manager is the steady-state owner of the shared shell, CLI environment,
87	and Moshi user unit. Ansible owns and deploys the ai-dev maintenance command,
88	builds the desired Home Manager activation package, compares it with the
89	current generation, and activates only when they differ. It then runs
90	`ai-dev-maintenance ensure-present`, which repairs missing tools without
91	updating installed tools. A second live run must report no changes when neither
92	repository's configuration has changed.
93	
94	## Interactive setup
95	
96	Home Manager owns OpenCode and the shared Fish, Starship, FZF, general Git
97	behavior, Hunk, Herdr, Yazi, and portable CLI configuration. Ansible deploys
98	`ai-dev-maintenance`, writes ai-dev's vaulted personal and BusinessCraft
99	identity fragments with mode `0600`, and selects the BusinessCraft fragment
100	below `~/businesscraft/`; the Mac retains its separate Home Manager-owned
101	identities.
102	
103	Run ongoing coding-agent updates deliberately on ai-dev:
104	
105	```sh
106	ai-dev-maintenance update
107	ai-dev-maintenance status
108	```
109	
110	The update command runs the official stable installers for Claude Code, Codex,
111	Pi, Herdr, and Moshi independently, updates the declared Pi packages,
112	reconciles Herdr before Moshi integrations, and reports all failures together.
113	Its implementation and ai-dev package inventory live in the Ansible role that
114	deploys it. Hermes is deliberately absent: it belongs to the separate `hermes`
115	account described below, not to the management user's toolchain.
116	The status command is read-only. Ansible does not copy SSH keys, OAuth sessions,
117	or API keys. Authenticate each tool interactively:
118	
119	```sh
120	gh auth login --hostname github.com --web --git-protocol ssh
121	claude
122	codex login --device-auth
123	pi
124	opencode auth login
125	```
126	
127	Authenticate the GitHub CLI as both required GitHub accounts. Before running
128	GitHub CLI operations for a repository under `~/businesscraft/`, select the
129	BusinessCraft account explicitly:
130	
131	```sh
132	gh auth switch --hostname github.com --user michaelmbc
133	gh auth status --hostname github.com
134	```
135	
136	Use `/login` inside Pi if it does not prompt automatically. Select a headless or
137	device-code provider flow when OpenCode offers one.
138	
139	Install Moshi on the approved phone, enable Tailscale, and run:
140	
141	```sh
142	moshi-hook host setup
143	moshi-hook pair --token <token-from-Moshi-Hooks-settings>
144	systemctl --user restart moshi-hook
145	moshi-hook install
146	```
147	
148	Scan the Easy Pair QR, save the MagicDNS host as `ai-dev`, and leave connection
149	mode on `Auto`. The gateway must remain on `127.0.0.1:24543`; OpenSSH permits
150	local TCP forwarding but disables gateway and Unix-socket forwarding.
151	
152	`ai-dev-maintenance` installs Herdr integrations before Moshi integrations so
153	their entries coexist. Check the complete toolchain and loopback-only Moshi
154	runtime after authentication:
155	
156	```sh
157	ai-dev-maintenance status
158	```
159	
160	Moshi's OpenCode hook is project-local. The maintenance command installs it in
161	the home workspace; run `moshi-hook install` once from each existing OpenCode
162	project root that should emit events. This repository does not inventory
163	untracked projects on the VM.
164	
165	Moshi's full agent integration sends limited notification summaries, approval
166	details, metadata, pairing, and WebSocket control traffic through Moshi's
167	service. Terminal traffic, source files, transcripts, and diffs remain direct.
168	
169	## Hermes infrastructure agent
170	
171	Hermes manages infrastructure, and it reads input nobody controls: web pages
172	through its bundled browser, and container logs, which are strings written by
173	whatever produced them. It therefore runs as its own `hermes` account, not as
174	the management user. `/home/michael` is mode `0750`, so the agent cannot read
175	the management user's GitHub tokens, SSH keys, or Claude and Codex sessions.
176	That separation is the point: scoping the agent's own credentials achieves
177	nothing while broader credentials sit beside it in the same home directory.
178	
179	Ansible owns the account, installs the agent with `--skip-setup`, and deploys
180	its credentials. The installer clones `NousResearch/hermes-agent` into
181	`~/.hermes/hermes-agent`, builds a uv virtualenv, links `~/.local/bin/hermes`,

content.text:
You were right to push back, and checking it turned up a real bug in my code. But the conclusion goes the other way: Tailscale SSH would break your setup, and you never had to paste keys anyway.

**Why Tailscale SSH is off — it's load-bearing, not an oversight**

Tailscale SSH isn't OpenSSH. It takes over port 22, and Mosh can't bootstrap through it, so you'd lose the UDP resilience that makes phone sessions survive network changes. It also doesn't implement `-L`/`-R` port forwarding at all, which kills both Plannotator reviews and Moshi's Browser Preview — the whole `19432` flow documented in this repo.

Moshi's own documentation says to turn Tailscale SSH off "so port 22 returns to the OS `sshd`", calling it simpler and more reliable. So your current setup already follows the vendor's recommendation. Enabling it would also fail the `RunSSH` assertion in `identity.yaml`.

**You don't paste keys**

This is the part that dissolves the concern. Moshi's Easy Pair appends *its own* public key to the target account's `authorized_keys` during pairing — that's how `michael` works today. No private key ever goes onto the phone. To reach the agent account you run the pairing flow again as `hermes`, which is a QR scan, not a key copy.

**The bug you flagged into existence**

Checking this, I found my `hermes` task wrote `authorized_keys` with `copy`, which replaces the whole file. That would have silently deleted Moshi's paired key on every subsequent Ansible run — you'd have paired the phone, then lost it at the next deploy, with nothing obvious to point at. The existing `common/users.yaml` avoids this by using `lineinfile` with a regexp scoped to the single operator key, so other entries survive. I've matched that pattern. Good catch on your part, even though it came from a different question.

I also recorded the rationale in `docs/ai-dev.md` — the port 22, Mosh, and forwarding reasons, plus the note that pairing provisions its own key — so the next person who asks "why not Tailscale SSH?" finds the answer instead of re-litigating it. The per-account pairing commands are in the "Reaching the agent" section.

All checks still pass: syntax, `ansible-lint` at production profile, shellcheck, and the maintenance test.

Still outstanding: the GitHub PAT, the two tailnet grants, and a deploy. Want the PR opened now?

exposure means moving those values out of Compose `environment:` entries, not
tightening the proxy. Treat the agent's credentials as revocable and rotate
them if ai-dev is ever suspect: delete the Proxmox token with
`pveum user token remove hermes-audit@pve ai-dev`, and revoke the GitHub token
in the GitHub UI.

## Plannotator remote reviews

Plannotator uses the fixed AI-Dev port `19432` with sharing disabled. Herdr
keeps Pi and its pending review alive, while the browser submits approval or
annotation feedback directly to Plannotator's HTTP decision interface.

listener.

On the laptop, inspect the effective client policy before the end-to-end test:

```sh
ssh -G ai-dev | grep -E \
  '^(user|localforward|exitonforwardfailure|identityagent|hashknownhosts) '
```

It must report user `michael`, forward-failure handling enabled, the
loopback-to-loopback `19432` forward, and the existing wildcard 1Password agent
and hashed-known-host settings.

## Agent scratch space

`/tmp` is a RAM-backed tmpfs carrying a per-user hard limit of 80% of its size
(1153 MiB at 4 GB RAM). Agent scratch exhausts that limit while `df` still shows
free space, and writes then fail with `EDQUOT`, which Node reports as the
unmapped `Unknown system error -122, write`.

Home Manager therefore sets `TMPDIR=/var/tmp/michael` for shells, and Ansible

1	# AI development VM
2	
3	`ai-dev` is the single AI development VM. It retains Proxmox VMID 110 and its
4	150 GB disk, with 4 CPU cores, fixed 5 GiB RAM, and an 8 GiB disk-backed
5	swapfile with a bounded zswap cache. Its only NIC is on the physical `vmbr1`
6	DMZ.
7	
8	The supported remote path is:
9	
10	```text
11	Moshi -> Tailscale private network -> OpenSSH -> Mosh when available -> Herdr
12	```
13	
14	Tailscale SSH stays disabled, and this is load-bearing rather than incidental.
15	Tailscale SSH is not OpenSSH: it takes over port 22, so Mosh cannot bootstrap
16	through it, and it does not implement `-L`/`-R` port forwarding, which Moshi's
17	Browser Preview depends on. Moshi's own
18	documentation recommends leaving it off so port 22 returns to the OS `sshd`.
19	Enabling it would break the path above and fail the identity assertions in the
20	ai-dev role.
21	
22	Disabling it costs nothing in key handling. Moshi's Easy Pair appends its own
23	public key to the target account's `authorized_keys` during pairing, so no
24	private key is ever pasted into the phone. Ansible manages only its own
25	operator key line, leaving Moshi's entry intact.
26	
27	Moshi connects to the guest's normal OpenSSH server through Tailscale, then
28	uses Mosh's per-connection UDP server when the network permits it. Herdr is the
29	only persistent multiplexer and retains its shared `Ctrl-A` prefix.
30	`Ctrl+Shift+L` is encoded as F12 by a supporting terminal, forwarded by Herdr,
31	and bound by Fish to clear the focused pane.
32	
33	## Deployment
34	
35	The existing guest initially advertises the old `ai-dev-bgd` MagicDNS name. For
36	the first Ansible run only, temporarily set the inventory line to:
37	
38	```ini
39	ai-dev ansible_host=ai-dev-bgd ansible_user=michael
40	```
41	
42	Run the AI host play, verify that Linux and Tailscale both advertise `ai-dev`,
43	then restore the committed inventory line without `ansible_host`. Do not leave
44	the migration alias in steady state.
45	
46	Before planning or applying Terraform, rotate any Tailscale authentication key
47	that was rendered into an old local cloud-init file. Remove the old
48	`terraform/files/ai-dev-bc.cfg` and `terraform/files/ai-dev-bgd.cfg` files after
49	rotation. They are ignored generated artifacts and must not be treated as a
50	credential store.
51	
52	Run:
53	
54	```sh
55	cd terraform
56	terraform fmt -check -recursive
57	terraform validate
58	terraform plan
59	```
60	
61	The plan must report the address move from
62	`module.ai_dev["ai-dev-bgd"]` to `module.ai_dev`, followed by an in-place rename
63	and CPU/memory update. Stop if VMID 110 or its disk would be destroyed or
64	replaced.
65	If the plan instead proposes creating all BPG-provider VMs or asks for the
66	legacy Telmate provider, stop: the local state predates the earlier provider
67	migration and must be reconciled/imported before this rename can be planned.
68	
69	Then stage the guest and router changes:
70	
71	```sh
72	cd ansible
73	ansible-playbook run.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass \
74	  --limit ai-dev --check --diff
75	ansible-playbook run.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass --limit ai-dev
76	ansible-playbook run.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass --limit ai-dev
77	cd ..
78	just routeros
79	```
80	
81	The ai-dev role clones the public `nix-config` repository to
82	`/home/michael/dev/nix-config`, fast-forwards it to `origin/main`, builds
83	`homeConfigurations."michael@ai-dev"`, and activates it as `michael`. A
84	non-fast-forward checkout or conflicting local change stops deployment.
85	Check mode builds the activation package but never activates it.
86	
87	Home Manager is the steady-state owner of the shared shell, CLI environment,
88	and Moshi user unit. Ansible owns and deploys the ai-dev maintenance command,
89	builds the desired Home Manager activation package, compares it with the
90	current generation, and activates only when they differ. It then runs
91	`ai-dev-maintenance ensure-present`, which repairs missing tools without
92	updating installed tools. A second live run must report no changes when neither
93	repository's configuration has changed.
94	
95	## Interactive setup
96	
97	Home Manager owns OpenCode and the shared Fish, Starship, FZF, general Git
98	behavior, Hunk, Herdr, Yazi, and portable CLI configuration. Ansible deploys
99	`ai-dev-maintenance`, writes ai-dev's vaulted personal and BusinessCraft
100	identity fragments with mode `0600`, and selects the BusinessCraft fragment
101	below `~/businesscraft/`; the Mac retains its separate Home Manager-owned
102	identities.
103	
104	Run ongoing coding-agent updates deliberately on ai-dev:
105	
106	```sh
107	ai-dev-maintenance update
108	ai-dev-maintenance status
109	```
110	
111	The update command runs the official stable installers for Claude Code, Codex,
112	Pi, Herdr, and Moshi independently, updates the declared Pi packages,
113	reconciles Herdr before Moshi integrations, and reports all failures together.
114	Its implementation and ai-dev package inventory live in the Ansible role that
115	deploys it. Hermes is deliberately absent: it belongs to the separate `hermes`
116	account described below, not to the management user's toolchain.
117	The status command is read-only. Ansible does not copy SSH keys, OAuth sessions,
118	or API keys. Authenticate each tool interactively:
119	
120	```sh
121	gh auth login --hostname github.com --web --git-protocol ssh
122	claude
123	codex login --device-auth
124	pi
125	opencode auth login
126	```
127	
128	Authenticate the GitHub CLI as both required GitHub accounts. Before running
129	GitHub CLI operations for a repository under `~/businesscraft/`, select the
130	BusinessCraft account explicitly:
131	
132	```sh
133	gh auth switch --hostname github.com --user michaelmbc
134	gh auth status --hostname github.com
135	```
136	
137	Use `/login` inside Pi if it does not prompt automatically. Select a headless or
138	device-code provider flow when OpenCode offers one.
139	
140	Install Moshi on the approved phone, enable Tailscale, and run:
141	
142	```sh
143	moshi-hook host setup
144	moshi-hook pair --token <token-from-Moshi-Hooks-settings>
145	systemctl --user restart moshi-hook
146	moshi-hook install
147	```
148	
149	Scan the Easy Pair QR, save the MagicDNS host as `ai-dev`, and leave connection
150	mode on `Auto`. The gateway must remain on `127.0.0.1:24543`; OpenSSH permits
151	local TCP forwarding but disables gateway and Unix-socket forwarding.
152	
153	`ai-dev-maintenance` installs Herdr integrations before Moshi integrations so
154	their entries coexist. Check the complete toolchain and loopback-only Moshi
155	runtime after authentication:
156	
157	```sh
158	ai-dev-maintenance status
159	```
160	
161	Moshi's OpenCode hook is project-local. The maintenance command installs it in
162	the home workspace; run `moshi-hook install` once from each existing OpenCode
163	project root that should emit events. This repository does not inventory
164	untracked projects on the VM.
165	
166	Moshi's full agent integration sends limited notification summaries, approval
167	details, metadata, pairing, and WebSocket control traffic through Moshi's
168	service. Terminal traffic, source files, transcripts, and diffs remain direct.
169	
170	## Hermes infrastructure agent
171	
172	Hermes manages infrastructure, and it reads input nobody controls: web pages
173	through its bundled browser, and container logs, which are strings written by
174	whatever produced them. It therefore runs as its own `hermes` account, not as
175	the management user. `/home/michael` is mode `0750`, so the agent cannot read
176	the management user's GitHub tokens, SSH keys, or Claude and Codex sessions.
177	That separation is the point: scoping the agent's own credentials achieves
178	nothing while broader credentials sit beside it in the same home directory.
179	
180	Ansible owns the account, installs the agent with `--skip-setup`, and deploys
181	its credentials. The installer clones `NousResearch/hermes-agent` into
182	`~/.hermes/hermes-agent`, builds a uv virtualenv, links `~/.local/bin/hermes`,

content.text:
Plannotator is fully removed — the spec doc deleted, the `19432` firewall assertion narrowed to the tailnet/DMZ checks that still matter, `@plannotator/pi-extension` dropped from `PI_PACKAGES`, and the docs section gone. Zero references remain, and all checks pass.

One thing I can't reach from here: `PLANNOTATOR_REMOTE`, `PLANNOTATOR_PORT` and `PLANNOTATOR_SHARE` are set by Home Manager, which lives in your separate `nix-config` repo. You'll want to strip them there too, or they'll keep being exported into every Fish session.

## Creating the PAT

Go to **github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens** → **Generate new token**. Make sure it's the *fine-grained* page, not the classic one.

- **Token name:** `ai-dev-hermes`
- **Resource owner:** `mich-murphy`
- **Expiration:** 90 days (fine-grained tokens can't be permanent; set a calendar reminder)
- **Repository access:** *Only select repositories* → `mich-murphy/home-infra`
- **Repository permissions:** set exactly two — **Contents: Read and write**, **Pull requests: Read and write**. Leave everything else at *No access*. GitHub adds **Metadata: Read-only** automatically; that's mandatory and fine.

Generate it and copy the `github_pat_…` value. Then vault it:

```
cd ansible
ansible-vault edit group_vars/secrets.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass
```

Add one line:

```yaml
hermes_github_token: "github_pat_..."
```

Contents write is what lets Hermes push a branch; Pull requests write is what lets it open the PR. Neither allows merging past your branch protection.

## Adding the Tailscale grants

Admin console → **Access controls**. Both destinations are untagged nodes, so a bare hostname in `dst` won't resolve — you need the `hosts` block first. I looked up the addresses:

```json
"hosts": {
  "docker-host": "100.96.174.126",
  "proxmox":     "100.106.15.105"
},
"grants": [
  {
    "src": ["tag:ai-dev"],
    "dst": ["docker-host"],
    "ip":  ["tcp:2375"]
  },
  {
    "src": ["tag:ai-dev"],
    "dst": ["proxmox"],
    "ip":  ["tcp:8006"]
  }
]
```

Merge those into your existing `hosts` and `grants` — don't replace the file, since your current SSH and Mosh grants need to stay. Save, and it takes effect immediately.

Keep these two the *only* grants with `tag:ai-dev` as a source. Grants are additive, so a broader one elsewhere silently overrides this narrowness — that's the failure mode worth watching for. Both are also in `docs/ai-dev.md` under "Tailnet policy" with the same warning.

Once both are in, the deploy sequence is `--check --diff`, then two live runs against ai-dev and docker-host.

Want me to open the PR now?

import pathlib

g = pathlib.Path('ansible/group_vars/ai_dev.yaml')
s = g.read_text()
old = """ai_dev_otel_collector_address: 100.96.174.126
ai_dev_otel_collector_port: 4318"""
new = """ai_dev_otel_collector_address: 100.96.174.126
ai_dev_otel_collector_port: 4318
# Hermes egress. ai-dev denies tailnet egress by default; these are the only
# two peers it may initiate sessions to, both read-only endpoints.
ai_dev_docker_proxy_address: 100.96.174.126
ai_dev_docker_proxy_port: 2375
ai_dev_proxmox_api_address: 100.106.15.105
ai_dev_proxmox_api_port: 8006"""
assert s.count(old) == 1
g.write_text(s.replace(old, new))

t = pathlib.Path('ansible/roles/ai-dev/templates/nftables.conf.j2')
ts = t.read_text()
old_rule = """    # Never initiate sessions to homelab or tailnet peers."""
new_rule = """    # Hermes reads the docker-host socket proxy and the Proxmox API. Both are
    # read-only endpoints, and these are the only tailnet peers ai-dev may
    # initiate sessions to.
    oifname "tailscale0" ip daddr {{ ai_dev_docker_proxy_address }} tcp dport {{ ai_dev_docker_proxy_port }} accept
    oifname "tailscale0" ip daddr {{ ai_dev_proxmox_api_address }} tcp dport {{ ai_dev_proxmox_api_port }} accept

1	# AI development VM
2	
3	`ai-dev` is the single AI development VM. It retains Proxmox VMID 110 and its
4	150 GB disk, with 4 CPU cores, fixed 5 GiB RAM, and an 8 GiB disk-backed
5	swapfile with a bounded zswap cache. Its only NIC is on the physical `vmbr1`
6	DMZ.
7	
8	The supported remote path is:
9	
10	```text
11	Moshi -> Tailscale private network -> OpenSSH -> Mosh when available -> Herdr
12	```
13	
14	Tailscale SSH stays disabled, and this is load-bearing rather than incidental.
15	Tailscale SSH is not OpenSSH: it takes over port 22, so Mosh cannot bootstrap
16	through it, and it does not implement `-L`/`-R` port forwarding, which Moshi's
17	Browser Preview depends on. Moshi's own documentation recommends leaving it off
18	so port 22 returns to the OS `sshd`.
19	Enabling it would break the path above and fail the identity assertions in the
20	ai-dev role.
21	
22	Disabling it costs nothing in key handling. Moshi's Easy Pair appends its own
23	public key to the target account's `authorized_keys` during pairing, so no
24	private key is ever pasted into the phone. Ansible manages only its own
25	operator key line, leaving Moshi's entry intact.
26	
27	Moshi connects to the guest's normal OpenSSH server through Tailscale, then
28	uses Mosh's per-connection UDP server when the network permits it. Herdr is the
29	only persistent multiplexer and retains its shared `Ctrl-A` prefix.
30	`Ctrl+Shift+L` is encoded as F12 by a supporting terminal, forwarded by Herdr,
31	and bound by Fish to clear the focused pane.
32	
33	## Deployment
34	
35	The existing guest initially advertises the old `ai-dev-bgd` MagicDNS name. For
36	the first Ansible run only, temporarily set the inventory line to:
37	
38	```ini
39	ai-dev ansible_host=ai-dev-bgd ansible_user=michael
40	```
41	
42	Run the AI host play, verify that Linux and Tailscale both advertise `ai-dev`,
43	then restore the committed inventory line without `ansible_host`. Do not leave
44	the migration alias in steady state.
45	
46	Before planning or applying Terraform, rotate any Tailscale authentication key
47	that was rendered into an old local cloud-init file. Remove the old
48	`terraform/files/ai-dev-bc.cfg` and `terraform/files/ai-dev-bgd.cfg` files after
49	rotation. They are ignored generated artifacts and must not be treated as a
50	credential store.
51	
52	Run:
53	
54	```sh
55	cd terraform
56	terraform fmt -check -recursive
57	terraform validate
58	terraform plan
59	```
60	
61	The plan must report the address move from
62	`module.ai_dev["ai-dev-bgd"]` to `module.ai_dev`, followed by an in-place rename
63	and CPU/memory update. Stop if VMID 110 or its disk would be destroyed or
64	replaced.
65	If the plan instead proposes creating all BPG-provider VMs or asks for the
66	legacy Telmate provider, stop: the local state predates the earlier provider
67	migration and must be reconciled/imported before this rename can be planned.
68	
69	Then stage the guest and router changes:
70	
71	```sh
72	cd ansible
73	ansible-playbook run.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass \
74	  --limit ai-dev --check --diff
75	ansible-playbook run.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass --limit ai-dev
76	ansible-playbook run.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass --limit ai-dev
77	cd ..
78	just routeros
79	```
80	
81	The ai-dev role clones the public `nix-config` repository to
82	`/home/michael/dev/nix-config`, fast-forwards it to `origin/main`, builds
83	`homeConfigurations."michael@ai-dev"`, and activates it as `michael`. A
84	non-fast-forward checkout or conflicting local change stops deployment.
85	Check mode builds the activation package but never activates it.
86	
87	Home Manager is the steady-state owner of the shared shell, CLI environment,
88	and Moshi user unit. Ansible owns and deploys the ai-dev maintenance command,
89	builds the desired Home Manager activation package, compares it with the
90	current generation, and activates only when they differ. It then runs
91	`ai-dev-maintenance ensure-present`, which repairs missing tools without
92	updating installed tools. A second live run must report no changes when neither
93	repository's configuration has changed.
94	
95	## Interactive setup
96	
97	Home Manager owns OpenCode and the shared Fish, Starship, FZF, general Git
98	behavior, Hunk, Herdr, Yazi, and portable CLI configuration. Ansible deploys
99	`ai-dev-maintenance`, writes ai-dev's vaulted personal and BusinessCraft
100	identity fragments with mode `0600`, and selects the BusinessCraft fragment
101	below `~/businesscraft/`; the Mac retains its separate Home Manager-owned
102	identities.
103	
104	Run ongoing coding-agent updates deliberately on ai-dev:
105	
106	```sh
107	ai-dev-maintenance update
108	ai-dev-maintenance status
109	```
110	
111	The update command runs the official stable installers for Claude Code, Codex,
112	Pi, Herdr, and Moshi independently, updates the declared Pi packages,
113	reconciles Herdr before Moshi integrations, and reports all failures together.
114	Its implementation and ai-dev package inventory live in the Ansible role that
115	deploys it. Hermes is deliberately absent: it belongs to the separate `hermes`
116	account described below, not to the management user's toolchain.
117	The status command is read-only. Ansible does not copy SSH keys, OAuth sessions,
118	or API keys. Authenticate each tool interactively:
119	
120	```sh
121	gh auth login --hostname github.com --web --git-protocol ssh
122	claude
123	codex login --device-auth
124	pi
125	opencode auth login
126	```
127	
128	Authenticate the GitHub CLI as both required GitHub accounts. Before running
129	GitHub CLI operations for a repository under `~/businesscraft/`, select the
130	BusinessCraft account explicitly:
131	
132	```sh
133	gh auth switch --hostname github.com --user michaelmbc
134	gh auth status --hostname github.com
135	```
136	
137	Use `/login` inside Pi if it does not prompt automatically. Select a headless or
138	device-code provider flow when OpenCode offers one.
139	
140	Install Moshi on the approved phone, enable Tailscale, and run:
141	
142	```sh
143	moshi-hook host setup
144	moshi-hook pair --token <token-from-Moshi-Hooks-settings>
145	systemctl --user restart moshi-hook
146	moshi-hook install
147	```
148	
149	Scan the Easy Pair QR, save the MagicDNS host as `ai-dev`, and leave connection
150	mode on `Auto`. The gateway must remain on `127.0.0.1:24543`; OpenSSH permits
151	local TCP forwarding but disables gateway and Unix-socket forwarding.
152	
153	`ai-dev-maintenance` installs Herdr integrations before Moshi integrations so
154	their entries coexist. Check the complete toolchain and loopback-only Moshi
155	runtime after authentication:
156	
157	```sh
158	ai-dev-maintenance status
159	```
160	
161	Moshi's OpenCode hook is project-local. The maintenance command installs it in
162	the home workspace; run `moshi-hook install` once from each existing OpenCode
163	project root that should emit events. This repository does not inventory
164	untracked projects on the VM.
165	
166	Moshi's full agent integration sends limited notification summaries, approval
167	details, metadata, pairing, and WebSocket control traffic through Moshi's
168	service. Terminal traffic, source files, transcripts, and diffs remain direct.
169	
170	## Hermes infrastructure agent
171	
172	Hermes manages infrastructure, and it reads input nobody controls: web pages
173	through its bundled browser, and container logs, which are strings written by
174	whatever produced them. It therefore runs as its own `hermes` account, not as
175	the management user. `/home/michael` is mode `0750`, so the agent cannot read
176	the management user's GitHub tokens, SSH keys, or Claude and Codex sessions.
177	That separation is the point: scoping the agent's own credentials achieves
178	nothing while broader credentials sit beside it in the same home directory.
179	
180	Ansible owns the account, installs the agent with `--skip-setup`, and deploys
181	its credentials. The installer clones `NousResearch/hermes-agent` into
182	`~/.hermes/hermes-agent`, builds a uv virtualenv, links `~/.local/bin/hermes`,

Both credentials and both grants are in place, and testing them surfaced a real gap in my work.

**What the test found**

Your grants are correct — `tailscale ping proxmox` succeeds, ai-dev carries `tag:ai-dev`, and both peers are visible. But a TCP connection to `proxmox:8006` times out, because ai-dev's own nftables output chain drops the entire `100.64.0.0/10` tailnet range. That rule is the strongest containment control on the guest, and I designed two new egress paths across this whole conversation without ever opening it. Your grants alone were never going to work.

Fixed by adding exactly two exceptions to `nftables.conf.j2`, alongside the existing MagicDNS and telemetry carve-outs, with the addresses declared in `group_vars/ai_dev.yaml` following the OTel collector's convention. The blanket drop stays. `firewall.yaml` now asserts both that the two endpoints are reachable *and* that the `100.64.0.0/10` drop survives beside them, so a future change can't quietly widen egress.

Incidentally, `ai_dev_otel_collector_address` is already docker-host — so ai-dev could reach that box on 4318 all along, just not on 2375.

**A correction to my earlier instructions**

I told you neither destination carried a tag. That was wrong — `tailscale status` shows `tag:proxmox` and `tag:server`. Your `hosts` block is still the right approach and needs no change, and I've documented why: `tag:server` covers more machines than docker-host, so scoping by host IP keeps the grant to the single machine you intended. The doc now says this instead of my incorrect claim.

I also added a note that the tailnet policy is necessary but not sufficient, naming this exact failure — a grant without the matching egress rule gives you a timeout with no obvious cause. That's an hour of debugging saved for whoever hits it next.

**Plannotator** is gone: spec doc deleted, the `19432` assertion narrowed to the tailnet and DMZ checks that still matter, and the Pi extension dropped. Remember `PLANNOTATOR_*` still needs removing from your `nix-config` repo, which I can't reach from here.

Gives the Hermes agent enough reach to diagnose the estate without giving it
the ability to change a running host, and keeps it out of the management
user's credentials.

## Why a separate account

Hermes ingests input nobody controls: web pages through its bundled browser,
and container logs, which are strings written by whatever produced them. It
now runs as its own `hermes` account. `/home/michael` is mode `0750`, so the
agent cannot read GitHub credentials, SSH keys, or Claude and Codex sessions.
Scoping the agent's own credentials achieves nothing while broader ones sit
beside it in the same home directory.

## Access tiers

| Tier | Reach | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Observe | Proxmox cluster and guest state | `PVEAuditor` API token |
| Observe | Containers, logs, stats, events | Read-only socket proxy |
| Propose | Any change to this repository | GitHub token, pull request only |
| Act | Nothing on a running host | Deliberately absent |

## Docker

A second `tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy` instance, same pinned image, kept
separate from Traefik's so widening the agent's read surface never widens
Traefik's. `POST=0` refuses every write route including exec and create.
Three independent controls stand in front of it:

1. it publishes only on `AGENT_PROXY_BIND`, docker-host's tailnet address,
   read at run time and written into `/srv/init/.env`;
2. the tailnet policy grants `tag:ai-dev` alone `tcp:2375`;
3. `DOCKER-USER` admits that one source address and drops every other client.

`verify.yaml` asserts the last two and asserts the container never binds all
interfaces — an empty `AGENT_PROXY_BIND` would otherwise make Compose bind
everywhere, silently.

## Egress

ai-dev's nftables output chain drops all of `100.64.0.0/10`. The two endpoints
above are added as explicit exceptions beside MagicDNS and the telemetry
collector, and the role asserts the blanket drop survives beside them. This
was found by testing: the tailnet grants alone produce a connection that times
out with no obvious cause.

## Known exposure

The socket proxy filters requests, not responses. `GET /containers/{id}/json`
returns a container's environment block, so the agent can read secrets passed
through Compose `environment:` entries. Removing that means moving those
values out of the environment; no proxy setting achieves it. Documented rather
than papered over.

## Plannotator

Removed as unused: specification document, Pi extension, port assertion, and
documentation. `PLANNOTATOR_*` shell variables still need removing from the
separate `nix-config` repository.

## Verification

`ansible-lint` passes at production profile, the playbook syntax-checks
against the real vault, `shellcheck` and the maintenance test pass, every
Compose file renders, and the Portainer drift check is clean. Not yet deployed
against a live host; the new firewall assertions prove the egress change on
first run.

## Follow-ups

- Rotate the Proxmox token once proven; it was created interactively during
  this work.
- A GitHub machine account would stop an owner-issued token merging past
  branch protection, which `enforce_admins: false` currently permits.
BODY

content.text:
You're not blocked — you just need the bypass, which is one flag:

```
gh pr merge 1730 --admin --squash
```

That's what `enforce_admins: false` buys you: as repo admin you can merge past the requirement. The web UI shows the same thing as a "Merge without waiting for requirements to be met" button. Wait for CI first, though — it's still running.

**Why I set it that way.** With one required approval, the agent cannot merge its own pull requests, because GitHub won't let anyone approve their own PR. That single flag is the entire thing standing between "Hermes proposes a change" and "Hermes edits a compose file, merges it, and Portainer deploys it to docker-host." Drop it to zero approvals and the agent's PAT — which has Contents write — can merge whatever it opens. The "Propose / Act" split in the PR table becomes fiction at that point.

So the friction is real, and it's load-bearing for you specifically because you're solo: there's no second human whose review is the natural gate.

**Three ways forward.** Keep it and merge with `--admin`, which costs one flag per PR and preserves the asymmetry. Or set up the machine account I flagged earlier — the agent authors PRs as a different identity, so you can approve them normally and only hit the bypass on your own PRs. Or drop the review requirement, accept that Hermes can self-merge, and rely on the fact that its PAT is scoped to this one repo.

I'd keep it as-is for now. `--admin` is cheap, and you can decide about the machine account once you've seen how often Hermes actually opens PRs.

One caveat I should be straight about, since it bears on whether this gate is worth anything: I flagged earlier that an owner-issued fine-grained PAT *might* be able to bypass branch protection too, since bypass is role-based. If that's true, the gate doesn't constrain Hermes at all and you're paying friction for nothing. I can settle it empirically — open a throwaway PR and try merging it with the agent's token, then close it. Takes a minute and tells us whether the machine account is optional or necessary. content.text:
Done — the PR now reports `CLEAN` instead of `BLOCKED`, so the normal merge button should work in the UI with no bypass needed.

What's still enforced: pull requests are required (no direct pushes to `main`), no force pushes, no branch deletion, linear history, and conversation resolution. What's gone: the approval requirement, and with it `dismiss_stale_reviews`, which no longer means anything at zero.

**The consequence, stated plainly.** Hermes's PAT has Contents write, which is what lets it push a branch — and the same permission lets it merge its own PR. GitHub doesn't separate those. So the "Propose / Act" split in that PR table is now a convention rather than an enforced boundary. It matters most for application stacks under `docker/`, because Portainer polls `main` and deploys those automatically: a self-merged compose change would reach docker-host without you touching anything. The `init` stack is safe either way, since Ansible owns it and only deploys when you run the playbook.

If you want that boundary back without the review friction, the cheapest fix isn't on GitHub's side at all — turn off Portainer's Git polling and let stack updates happen on a webhook or manual pull. Then a merge never deploys by itself, whoever made it. That's one setting per stack and it restores the human step where it actually matters. Happy to look at that when you're ready, or leave it.

I'd still suggest the machine account eventually, since it's the only thing that makes the distinction real, but it's reasonable to wait until you've seen how Hermes actually behaves.

Merge whenever you're ready — CI is green. After that, `--limit docker-host` first, then `--limit ai-dev`, with a check run before each.

content.text:
Good catch to check, but that specific one is safe — and you've surfaced a real inconsistency elsewhere.

`AGENT_PROXY_BIND: 100.64.0.1` is a placeholder I invented for CI: it's the first address of the `100.64.0.0/10` CGNAT range that Tailscale draws from, not an address on your tailnet. CI only needs *something* shaped like an IP so Compose renders a valid port binding.

But yes, the PR does add two real ones:

- **`100.96.174.126`** (docker-host) — already public. It's been on `main` as `ai_dev_otel_collector_address` in `group_vars/ai_dev.yaml`. The PR adds two more references.
- **`100.106.15.105`** (proxmox) — **new disclosure**, in `group_vars/ai_dev.yaml` and `docs/ai-dev.md`.

On exposure: these are CGNAT addresses, routable only inside your tailnet and meaningless to anyone without access to it. So the practical risk is recon value, not reachability — it confirms which hosts exist and roughly how the tailnet is laid out.

The part that bothers me more is my own inconsistency. In `bootstrap-stack.yaml` I read docker-host's tailnet address at run time and wrote a comment saying explicitly *"not committed: this repository is public"* — then hardcoded two tailnet addresses into `group_vars` a few commits later. Both reasonings can't be right.

Three ways to square it, and I'd pick the third:

Leave it, on the grounds that the otel address set the precedent already. Or resolve both at run time via `tailscale ip -4 <host>`, which puts no IPs in the repo but couples ai-dev's firewall run to MagicDNS resolving two peers — if docker-host is down, the play fails. Or move both into `group_vars/secrets.yaml`, which is exactly what this repo already does for the RouterOS reservation MACs, with the comment *"Reservation MACs live in vaulted secrets.yaml"* recording the same concern. No runtime coupling, no public IPs, and an established pattern.

Want me to move them to the vault? It's a small change to #1730, and I'd move the pre-existing otel address too so the three are handled the same way.

content.text:
The IPs are out of PR #1730, but I need to flag something you'll hit.

**On "are these even needed"** — the addresses themselves are, the *committed* ones aren't. nftables rules match on literal IPs, and we proved empirically that without the egress rule you get a silent timeout. So I switched to resolving both with `tailscale ip -4` during the play, which is what I already do for docker-host's bind address, with an assertion that each resolves to exactly one tailnet address before egress opens. `group_vars` now holds hostnames, and the docs show the command instead of the values.

The branch adds no real tailnet addresses now. What's left is `100.64.0.0/10`, the CGNAT range, and `100.64.0.1`, the CI placeholder — neither is a host on your tailnet.

**The thing you'll hit:** I tested merging the two branches and they conflict, in `group_vars/ai_dev.yaml` and `nftables.conf.j2`. Your otel-removal commit on #1731 deletes lines that #1730 edits right beside. Whichever merges second needs a manual resolution.

Since your otel change and my egress change touch the same two spots, the cleanest fix is to merge #1731 first, then rebase #1730 onto the updated `main` — my rules sit where the otel rule used to be, so the result is one clean block instead of an interleaved diff. I can do that rebase once you've merged #1731.

CI on #1730 is still running `ansible` and `terraform`; the other three pass.

One more thing worth a moment: removing the otel collector egress means anything on ai-dev that was shipping telemetry to `:4318` stops silently. If that was wired up deliberately, worth confirming nothing still depends on it before merging #1731.

#!/usr/sbin/nft -f

flush ruleset

table inet filter {
  chain input {
    type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;

    ct state established,related accept
    iifname "lo" accept

    # Moshi reaches normal OpenSSH and mosh only through the tailnet.
    iifname "tailscale0" tcp dport 22 accept
    iifname "tailscale0" udp dport 60000-61000 accept
    iifname "tailscale0" drop

    # DHCP is the only unsolicited input accepted from the physical DMZ.
    iifname "{{ ai_dev_physical_interface }}" ip saddr {{ ai_dev_dmz_gateway }} udp sport 67 udp dport 68 accept
    iifname "{{ ai_dev_physical_interface }}" drop
  }

  chain forward {
    type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop;
  }

  chain output {
    type filter hook output priority 0; policy drop;

    ct state established,related accept
    oifname "lo" accept

    # The guest may acquire a lease and use only the router-advertised DNS service.
    oifname "{{ ai_dev_physical_interface }}" ip daddr { {{ ai_dev_dmz_gateway }}, 255.255.255.255 } udp sport 68 udp dport 67 accept
    oifname "{{ ai_dev_physical_interface }}" ip daddr {{ ai_dev_dns_server }} udp dport 53 accept
    oifname "{{ ai_dev_physical_interface }}" ip daddr {{ ai_dev_dns_server }} tcp dport 53 accept

    # Tailscale's local MagicDNS resolver is infrastructure, not a peer.
    oifname "tailscale0" ip daddr 100.100.100.100 udp dport 53 accept
    oifname "tailscale0" ip daddr 100.100.100.100 tcp dport 53 accept

1	# AI development VM
2	
3	`ai-dev` is the single AI development VM. Its only NIC is on the physical
4	`vmbr1` DMZ, and it carries an 8 GiB disk-backed swapfile with a bounded zswap
5	cache. `terraform/main.tf` holds its current spec.
6	
7	The supported remote path is:
8	
9	```text
10	Moshi -> Tailscale private network -> OpenSSH -> Mosh when available -> Herdr
11	```
12	
13	Tailscale SSH stays disabled, and this is load-bearing rather than incidental.
14	Tailscale SSH is not OpenSSH: it takes over port 22, so Mosh cannot bootstrap
15	through it, and it does not implement `-L`/`-R` port forwarding, which Moshi's
16	Browser Preview depends on. Moshi's own documentation recommends leaving it off
17	so port 22 returns to the OS `sshd`. Enabling it would break the path above and
18	fail the identity assertions in the ai-dev role.
19	
20	Disabling it costs nothing in key handling. Moshi's Easy Pair appends its own
21	public key to the target account's `authorized_keys` during pairing, so no
22	private key is ever pasted into the phone. Ansible manages only its own
23	operator key line, leaving Moshi's entry intact.
24	
25	Herdr is the only persistent multiplexer on the guest.
26	
27	## Deployment
28	
29	Generated cloud-init files under `terraform/files/` are ignored build
30	artifacts, not a credential store: rotate any Tailscale authentication key that
31	was rendered into one.
32	
33	Run:
34	
35	```sh
36	cd terraform
37	terraform fmt -check -recursive
38	terraform validate
39	terraform plan
40	```
41	
42	Stop if VMID 110 or its disk would be destroyed or replaced; `main.tf` keeps a
43	`moved` block, so an address move is the only structural change a plan should
44	ever report here.
45	If the plan instead proposes creating all BPG-provider VMs or asks for the
46	legacy Telmate provider, stop: the local state predates the earlier provider
47	migration and must be reconciled/imported before this rename can be planned.
48	
49	Then stage the guest and router changes:
50	
51	```sh
52	cd ansible
53	ansible-playbook run.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass \
54	  --limit ai-dev --check --diff
55	ansible-playbook run.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass --limit ai-dev
56	ansible-playbook run.yaml --vault-password-file .vaultpass --limit ai-dev
57	cd ..
58	just routeros
59	```
60	
61	The ai-dev role builds and activates Home Manager from the public `nix-config`
62	repository. A non-fast-forward checkout or conflicting local change stops
63	deployment; check mode builds the activation package but never activates it.
64	
65	Home Manager is the steady-state owner of the shared shell, CLI environment,
66	and Moshi user unit. Ansible owns and deploys the ai-dev maintenance command,
67	builds the desired Home Manager activation package, compares it with the
68	current generation, and activates only when they differ. It then runs
69	`ai-dev-maintenance ensure-present`, which repairs missing tools without
70	updating installed tools. A second live run must report no changes when neither
71	repository's configuration has changed.
72	
73	## Interactive setup
74	
75	Home Manager owns the portable CLI configuration. Ansible deploys
76	`ai-dev-maintenance` and writes the vaulted git identity fragments, selecting
77	the BusinessCraft one below `~/businesscraft/`.
78	
79	Run ongoing coding-agent updates deliberately on ai-dev:
80	
81	```sh
82	ai-dev-maintenance update
83	ai-dev-maintenance status
84	```
85	
86	The update command runs the official stable installers for Claude Code, Codex,
87	Pi, Herdr, and Moshi independently, updates the declared Pi packages,
88	reconciles Herdr before Moshi integrations, and reports all failures together.
89	Its implementation and ai-dev package inventory live in the Ansible role that
90	deploys it. Hermes is deliberately absent: it belongs to the separate `hermes`
91	account described below, not to the management user's toolchain.
92	The status command is read-only. Ansible does not copy SSH keys, OAuth sessions,
93	or API keys. Authenticate each tool interactively:
94	
95	```sh
96	gh auth login --hostname github.com --web --git-protocol ssh
97	claude
98	codex login --device-auth
99	pi
100	opencode auth login
101	```
102	
103	Authenticate the GitHub CLI as both required GitHub accounts. Before running
104	GitHub CLI operations for a repository under `~/businesscraft/`, select the
105	BusinessCraft account explicitly:
106	
107	```sh
108	gh auth switch --hostname github.com --user <businesscraft-account>
109	gh auth status --hostname github.com
110	```
111	
112	Use `/login` inside Pi if it does not prompt automatically. Select a headless or
113	device-code provider flow when OpenCode offers one.
114	
115	Pair Moshi from the phone with `moshi-hook host setup` and `moshi-hook pair`.
116	The gateway must remain on `127.0.0.1:24543`: OpenSSH permits local TCP
117	forwarding but disables gateway and Unix-socket forwarding. Its OpenCode hook
118	is project-local, so run `moshi-hook install` once from each project root that
119	should emit events.
120	
121	## Hermes infrastructure agent
122	
123	Hermes manages infrastructure, and it reads input nobody controls: web pages
124	through its bundled browser, and container logs, which are strings written by
125	whatever produced them. It therefore runs as its own `hermes` account, not as
126	the management user. `/home/michael` is mode `0750`, so the agent cannot read
127	the management user's GitHub tokens, SSH keys, or Claude and Codex sessions.
128	That separation is the point: scoping the agent's own credentials achieves
129	nothing while broader credentials sit beside it in the same home directory.
130	
131	Ansible owns the account, installs the agent with `--skip-setup`, and deploys
132	its credentials. The installer clones `NousResearch/hermes-agent` into
133	`~/.hermes/hermes-agent`, builds a uv virtualenv, links `~/.local/bin/hermes`,
134	and pulls a Hermes-managed Node and a Playwright browser, so the first run is
135	long and the install is the largest on the VM. ai-dev installs the Docker
136	client for `DOCKER_HOST` queries but masks `docker.service` and
137	`docker.socket`; it must never run a daemon of its own.
138	
139	### Access tiers
140	
141	The agent observes broadly, acts narrowly, and proposes everything else.
142	
143	| Tier | Reach | Mechanism |
144	| --- | --- | --- |
145	| Observe | Proxmox cluster and guest state | `PVEAuditor` API token |
146	| Observe | Containers, logs, stats, events | Read-only socket proxy |
147	| Propose | Any change to this repository | GitHub token, pull request only |
148	| Act | Nothing on a running host | Deliberately absent |
149	
150	No credential the agent holds can change a running host. Remediation happens
151	by pull request, which `main`'s branch protection forces through review, and
152	which Portainer then deploys. A merge is the supervision that a watched SSH
153	session used to provide.
154	
155	### Provisioning the credentials
156	
157	Two credentials are minted by hand and kept in the Ansible vault: a Proxmox
158	API token holding `PVEAuditor` with privilege separation, which is read-only by
159	construction, and a fine-grained GitHub token scoped to this repository alone
160	with Contents and Pull requests read/write and nothing else. Fine-grained
161	tokens cannot be minted through the API, so that one is created in the GitHub
162	UI. `ansible/roles/ai-dev/defaults/main.yaml` names the vault keys the role
163	reads.
164	
165	The play installs the agent without these and reports their absence, so the
166	host can be provisioned before the tokens exist. With them present it writes
167	`~hermes/.config/hermes/env` at mode `0600`, sourced from the account's
168	`.profile`.
169	
170	### Reaching the agent
171	
172	The account is a normal login. Ansible authorizes the same operator key that
173	reaches the management user and enables linger, so the account can hold its
174	own persistent Herdr and Moshi services. Either path works:
175	
176	```sh
177	ssh hermes@ai-dev          # dedicated session, own Herdr and Moshi
178	sudo -u hermes -i          # from an existing management-user pane
179	```
180

content.text:
Found the cause, and it isn't what it looked like.

**The 88 warnings were systemd, not Ansible or fish.** The escape is `OSC 3008`, systemd's "Hierarchical Context Signalling" — the full marker reads `comm=sudo;targetuser=root;type=session`. sudo emits it to describe the privilege transition, but only when a TTY is attached. Ansible allocates a TTY for `become`, so every privileged task got one appended after its JSON, and Ansible warned about the trailing bytes. That's why plain `ssh host 'echo hi'` looked clean and `ansible -m ping` was clean too — only `ansible -m ping -b` reproduced it.

**Fix: `pipelining = True`** in `ansible.cfg`. It sends the module over the existing SSH session with no TTY, so sudo stays quiet. It also drops a temp file write per task, so runs get noticeably faster. I verified it works against docker-host as well; `unifi-controller` is unreachable either way, which is pre-existing and unrelated to this.

I'm re-running the full check now to confirm zero warnings.

**Separately, that run also failed** — one task, unrelated to the warnings:

```
TASK [ai-dev : Require a clean Nix configuration worktree]
Refusing to deploy with local changes in /home/michael/dev/nix-config.
```

That's the role's guard doing its job, not a bug. `/home/michael/dev/nix-config` on ai-dev has uncommitted changes, and the role won't build Home Manager from a dirty tree. Worth knowing it stops the play at task 90 of ~122, so the Hermes tasks never ran — this check has told you nothing yet about the new agent account or the firewall assertions. You'll need to commit, stash, or discard those changes on ai-dev before the deploy can prove anything.
